# Variables and expressions

Now let's take a look how Quarto notebooks work with Julia:

```{julia}
# Assigning variables
a = 3
b = 4

# Arithmetic
c = a^2 + b^2
```

Note that the last assigned object is shown in the notebook. This can be annoying, but you can avoid it doing the following:

```{julia}
# Assigning variables
a = 3
b = 4

# Arithmetic
c = a^2 + b^2;
```

Also you can explicitly print out stuff:

```{julia}
println("Hello")
println(2+5);
```

# Functions

Functions are central in Julia. They can take multiple arguments, optional arguments, and return multiple values.

```{julia}
function hypotenuse(a, b)
    return sqrt(a^2 + b^2)
end

# One-line function
square(x) = x^2

# Anonymous function
cube = x -> x^3

println(hypotenuse(3,4))
println(square(5))
println(cube(2))
println((square(5),cube(2)))

# Multiple arguments
function weighted_average(x, y, w1, w2)
    return (w1*x + w2*y) / (w1 + w2)
end

println(weighted_average(10, 20, 2, 1))

# Optional arguments
function power(x, p=2)
    return x^p
end

println(power(3))
println(power(3,3))

# Keyword arguments
function greet(name; polite=true)
    if polite
        return "Hello, $name. Nice to meet you!"
    else
        return "Hey $name"
    end
end

println((greet("Alice"), greet("Bob"; polite=false)))

#Multiple Outputs
function minmax(v)
    return minimum(v), maximum(v)
end

vals = [3, 7, 2, 9, 5]
mn, mx = minmax(vals)

println(mn)
println(mx)
```

# Loops

Very useful for dynamic programming

```{julia}
n = 10
s = 0
for i in 1:n
    println(s)
    s += i
end

#While loops
function factorial(n)
    f = 1
    i = 1
    while i <= n
        f *= i
        i += 1
    end
    return f
end
println(factorial(5))

#Break loop
function lower_than_n(n)
    for i = 1:100
        println("Let's analyze $i")
        if i<n
            println("$i is lower than $n, so we keep going!")
        else
            println("$i is equal to $n, so we stop!")
            break
        end
    end
end
println(lower_than_n(7))
```

# Vectorize

Vectorizing certain operations has a different syntax in Julia. Here are some examples of this:

```{julia}
v = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

# Square each element
v_squared = v .^ 2

# Add two vectors element-wise
u = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
v_plus_u = v .+ u

# Apply a function element-wise
exp_v = exp.(v)

(v_squared, v_plus_u, exp_v)
```

# Optimization

```{julia}

x = [3, 7, 2, 9, 5]

m = maximum(x)      # Maximum value
pos = argmax(x)     # Position of maximum value

println((m, pos))

# Matrix
A = [3 7 2;
     9 5 1]

# Maximum of entire matrix
m_all = maximum(A)

# Position of maximum value (linear index)
pos_all = argmax(A)

# Find both value and position at once
val, pos = findmax(A)

println((m_all, pos_all, val, pos, A[pos]))

# Maximum per row (broadcasting over each row as a vector)
row_max = [maximum(row) for row in eachrow(A)]
row_argmax = [argmax(row) for row in eachrow(A)]

# Maximum per column (broadcasting over each column as a vector)
col_max = [maximum(col) for col in eachcol(A)]
col_argmax = [argmax(col) for col in eachcol(A)]

println((row_max, row_argmax, col_max, col_argmax))

```
